item.title: America's biggest beer-loving states revealed — see where yours ranks
item.description: America's beer capital runs through Wisconsin for the second straight year, with the Midwest dubbed the nation's "beer belt." Regional loyalty remains strong, experts say.
item.content:encoded:
Beer has a storied history in the United States and was a common beverage in colonial America. Its influence on the nation's culture remains strong – and a new study found which states appear to be most interested in beer.

"Wisconsin is still America's beer capital," reported consumer research firm Innerbody Research in the website's recently released analysis of a year's worth of Google Trends search data.

This marks the second year in a row the Badger State came out on top in the rankings. Innerbody labeled the Midwest "America's beer belt," since "Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota and Missouri all rank among the nation's top 10," and "every Midwestern state finishes in the top 20."

GEORGE WASHINGTON'S 1757 BEER RECIPE BROUGHT BACK TO LIFE AHEAD OF AMERICA'S 250TH BIRTHDAY

"The Midwest is one of many regions with a deep historic beer culture tied to both a long legacy of regional production and reinvigorated by craft brewers in recent decades," Bart Watson, president and CEO of the Colorado-based Brewers Association, told Fox News Digital.

Wyoming came in second place for its search-interest score. Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa came in third, fourth and fifth, respectively.

States along the Pacific coast showed lower beer-related search interest, according to the study. Alaska, Washington, California, Oregon and Hawaii were in the bottom 10 for beer searches.

When it comes to specific brands, regional loyalty remains strong.

"The local dominance of a beer brand is almost entirely driven by historic entry advantage," Jean-Pierre H. Dubé, a marketing professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, who has published research explaining the regional dominance of brands, told Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Miller dominates in Wisconsin because it was first to market there. In contrast, Budweiser was first to market in St. Louis, where it also remains dominant. The prevalence of beer tastes in the Midwest reflects the fact that most of the world's largest brewers in the late 1800s were in the Midwest in St. Louis, Wisconsin and Chicago – but especially Wisconsin."

Samuel Adams "launched in Boston and was arguably the first successful craft brewer to become a dominant brand and obtain national distribution," Dubé added.

Michelob Ultra generated the most search interest among the beer brands analyzed and also came out on top in Alabama, Nevada and Oklahoma.

"One of beer's strengths is the many options for lower calories and ABV relative to other adult beverages," Watson said. 

"Light beers underline that quality and have been very popular ever since they were introduced. In recent years, interest in particular attributes, like low-carb beers, has also been a factor in consumer preferences."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Stella Artois was the most popular beer in Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois, Louisiana, New York, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia and Washington, D.C.

Along with other imported beers, Stella is "perceived as a premium beer in the U.S.," though that isn't its reputation in the brand's home market of Belgium, Dubé said.

Dubé's studies have found that exposure to certain beers when consumers first reach legal drinking age influences what they prefer later in life.

"Millennials in cities with few craft brands at 21 drink way more national-brand beer today – Bud and Miller – than millennials in cities with relatively more craft beer brands when they came of age," he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Beer Marketer Insights reported this year that Michelob Ultra had overtaken Bud Light and Modelo Especial to become the top-selling beer in the U.S. by volume.

Sales and search aren't perfectly correlated, Watson said, and the Innerbody findings "signal something about new interest and brands as much as overall brand strength or sales."

"A sales map would undoubtedly look very different," he said. "At the end of the day, beer is supposed to be fun, so no one should take them too seriously, and they are best argued over with friends and family with a beer in hand."

item.title: JD Vance's mother Beverly Vance reacts to vice president's 'childless cat ladies' spat with Taylor Swift
item.description: Beverly Vance said she had no idea Taylor Swift referenced JD Vance's "childless cat ladies" comment in her Kamala Harris endorsement post online.
item.content:encoded:
Vice President JD Vance’s comment about "childless cat ladies" became a talking point during President Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign. Taylor Swift even referenced it when she endorsed Kamala Harris and Tim Walz.

Yet Beverly Vance, JD Vance's mother, had no idea Swift had taken a shot at her son over his "childless cat ladies" comment.

"I had no idea that's what she was even doing. Until you just said that, I didn't even put the two together," Vance said with a laugh during a recent appearance on OutKick’s "Tomi Lahren is Fearless."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

JD Vance appeared on Fox News for an interview with Tucker Carlson in 2021, and the then-Senate candidate said that Democrats are "a bunch of childless cat ladies who are miserable at their own lives and the choices that they've made and so they want to make the rest of the country miserable, too."

Beverly said her son meant it as a joke and cited his sense of humor.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

"I just thought it was funny," Beverly said. "JD's just got a sense of humor and you know he was making a joke and obviously people didn't take it as a joke, but you know, I know JD and he just meant it as a joke."

The vice president admitted his comment was a mistake in his book. In Swift’s post endorsing Harris and Walz, she posed for a photo with a cat.

Tomi Lahren mentioned that Swift’s husband, Kansas City Chiefs superstar Travis Kelce, grew up in Ohio, like the Vances. Beverly quickly pointed out that Kelce played college football at the University of Cincinnati.

item.title: AMB. GORDON SONDLAND: The Godfather Test -- How Putin turns every attack into a mystery—and gets away with it
item.description: Former Amb. Gordon Sondland's 'Godfather Test' urges NATO and the European Union to presume Vladimir Putin is behind cyberattacks and sabotage targeting the West.
item.content:encoded:
In one of the most memorable scenes in "The Godfather," Don Vito Corleone gathers the heads of New York’s crime families to make peace and secure the return of his son Michael.

"But I’m a superstitious man," he tells them.

He then warns that if Michael should suffer some supposedly random misfortune—an implausible suicide, a fatal accident or even a bolt of lightning—"then I’m going to blame some of the people in this room…"

RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS

The message was unmistakable: Do not hide an attack behind coincidence, an intermediary or a carefully manufactured lack of proof. Whatever disguise is chosen, I will know where it came from, and I will hold the responsible people accountable.

It is time for NATO and the European Union to adopt what might be called the Godfather Test.

If a drone mysteriously crosses into the territory of an Eastern European country, we should presume Vladimir Putin is responsible.

If a power cable is severed beneath the Baltic Sea, we should presume Vladimir Putin is responsible.

US INTEL WARNS RUSSIA COULD LAUNCH LIMITED ATTACK ON NATO ALLY IN EFFORT TO FRAGMENT ORGANIZATION: REPORT

If a government network is crippled, a weapons factory explodes, a railway system is disrupted or a political figure suddenly becomes the beneficiary of a sophisticated disinformation campaign, we should presume Vladimir Putin is responsible.

Putin can then prove that he was not.

This reverses the way the West has traditionally approached such events. Our democracies are built upon the presumption of innocence. It is one of our most important values, and it must remain inviolate when we administer justice to individuals through our courts.

But Vladimir Putin is not a defendant standing in an American courtroom. Russia is not entitled to the protections of the Bill of Rights, a jury of its peers or an endless international discovery process before the West acts to defend itself.

We have no obligation to presume that the Kremlin is innocent while it is accorded some imaginary form of geopolitical due process. Yet that is effectively what we have been doing. Russia exploits our own system of innocence until guilt is proven, turning one of democracy’s greatest virtues into a strategic vulnerability.

I’M PRESIDENT OF ONE OF AMERICA’S MOST RELIABLE ALLIES. HERE’S HOW WE STAND UP TO RUSSIA

The Kremlin understands that Western governments are reluctant to act without evidence that can be publicly disclosed and defended beyond a reasonable doubt. So Russia structures its operations to ensure that such evidence will rarely exist—or cannot be revealed without compromising intelligence sources and methods.

Putin forfeited the benefit of the doubt long ago.

He forfeited it through the invasion of neighboring countries, the use of proxies and cutouts, cyberattacks, political interference, assassinations, sabotage, energy coercion and an endless stream of denials that collapses under scrutiny only after the damage is done.

A government that repeatedly commits arson should not be treated as an innocent bystander every time smoke rises from another building.

GERMANY BLAMES RUSSIA AFTER EXPLOSIVE-LADEN DRONE FOUND NEAR UKRAINIAN CARGO PLANES AT MAJOR AIRPORT

For years, Russia has operated inside the gray zone between peace and open warfare. Its actions are designed to be damaging enough to weaken its adversaries but sufficiently murky to prevent a decisive response. Moscow uses anonymous hackers, commercial vessels, intelligence operatives, fabricated local movements and supposedly independent criminal organizations. It obscures responsibility, demands impossible standards of proof and then ridicules the West for its uncertainty.

The tactic works because we allow it to work.

Every incident is treated as an entirely new mystery. Governments open investigations, consult experts, compare intelligence and debate attribution. Months pass. The public loses interest. Allies disagree over whether the evidence clears some arbitrary threshold. Russia denies everything, and the matter quietly disappears.

By then, the Kremlin has already moved on to its next operation.

NATO ALLY POLAND WARNS RUSSIA, BELARUS PUSHING ILLEGAL MIGRANTS TOWARD ALLIANCE — AND THE US

Our excessive caution does not make us judicious. It makes us predictable. Putin knows that unless he launches a conventional attack with Russian flags flying from every tank, NATO will argue with itself over whether he was really responsible. That hesitation is not an unfortunate side effect of his strategy. It is the central objective.

The West must reverse both the presumption and the incentive.

When suspicious acts of sabotage or destabilization threaten NATO or EU countries and bear the hallmarks of Russian activity, Moscow should be treated as responsible unless persuasive evidence demonstrates otherwise.

REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES

And each event should be met with an asymmetric ratcheting up of the costs imposed on Russia.

If the Kremlin damages a cable, we need not damage a Russian cable. If it attacks a government computer network, we need not attack an identical network in return. Symmetrical retaliation allows Putin to calculate the price in advance and treat it as merely another cost of doing business.

Our response should instead occur in an area Putin values, at a time of our choosing and at a cost greater than the benefit Russia obtained from its original attack.

TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO SPEND BIG — NOW COMES THE HARDER QUESTION: CAN EUROPE ACTUALLY FIGHT?

That might mean quietly disabling a Russian military capability, compromising an intelligence network, obstructing a revenue stream, exposing hidden assets, disrupting sanctions evasion or increasing the effectiveness of Ukrainian operations. The precise response should depend upon the circumstances, but the governing formula must be simple: every act of Russian mischief leaves the Kremlin worse off than it was before.

Nor should we feel compelled to announce what we have done.

RUSSIA THREATENS STRIKES ON UK MILITARY TARGETS, ‘CATASTROPHIC CONSEQUENCES’ OVER UKRAINE

Russia does not hold a press conference after every cyberattack, act of sabotage or covert operation. Neither should we. There is no strategic virtue in providing Putin with a detailed accounting of our capabilities, methods and decision-making.

We should be as quiet about our response as Russia is about its attack.

Putin should know that a price has been paid, but he need not always know precisely when, where or how it was imposed. Uncertainty has been one of his most effective weapons. It is time for the West to use uncertainty as well.

NATO'S EASTERN FLANK RACES TO REARM AS TRUMP PRESSURE EXPOSES WESTERN EUROPE'S DEFENSE GAP

This does not mean responding impulsively to every electrical failure, industrial accident or unexplained drone. Intelligence still matters. Judgment still matters. Allied coordination still matters. The presumption should be strong, not mindless.

But we must stop requiring courtroom-grade proof before defending countries and institutions that are not courtrooms. National security decisions have always been made using intelligence assessments, patterns of conduct, capabilities, motives and probabilities. Absolute certainty is rarely available—and insisting upon it simply gives the aggressor a veto over our response.

Some will object that this creates a risk of miscalculation. Of course, it does. But our present policy creates a much larger risk: that Putin will continue escalating because he believes the West is institutionally incapable of responding to anything short of a full-scale invasion.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Deterrence is not achieved by proving responsibility to a mathematical certainty months after every attack. It is achieved by convincing an adversary beforehand that his actions will carry consequences.

Europe has spent decades constructing elaborate legal and diplomatic processes while Putin has spent those same decades learning how to manipulate them. He understands that democratic governments fear acting on incomplete information. He therefore ensures that the information will always be incomplete.

We should stop rewarding him for his craftsmanship.

The presumption should now be simple. If serious misfortune befalls one of the countries in Putin’s sights—through a drone, a cyberattack, a mysterious explosion, a damaged pipeline or some other extraordinarily convenient accident—we are going to blame the man in the room who has repeatedly threatened us, attacked his neighbors and perfected the art of deniable aggression.

Then we will respond asymmetrically, quietly and with enough force to ensure that the next act of mischief costs him even more—even if we fail to meet the "beyond a reasonable doubt" hurdle.

item.title: Dementia stole my grandmother from us. I am fighting to give families more time
item.description: After losing her grandmother to vascular dementia in Queens, New York, one advocate now leads the push for earlier Alzheimer's diagnosis nationwide.
item.content:encoded:
My big, Italian family revolved around my grandmother: a feisty daughter of immigrants fighting for the American dream in Queens, New York. No one was a stranger in her home; she cooked, laughed, and welcomed everyone. My mother joked that the boys she brought home ended up falling in love with my grandmother, instead. Always bold and unapologetic, Grandma would take us to the movie theater and shout commentary over the dialogue as we muffled our embarrassed laughter.

Then, something changed. In 2006, my once-lively grandmother was diagnosed with vascular dementia. It was devastating news, but it also finally answered questions we'd been asking for years. The woman who had always been the center of our family was beginning to shrink inward. My mother, her caregiver, did everything she could to preserve Grandma's joyful spirit, but she grew quiet and withdrawn, overwhelmed by the very gatherings she'd once loved. My grandmother lived with dementia for nearly a decade before passing away in October 2016.

Watching her decline drew me into the fight against Alzheimer’s disease, the most common form of dementia and the only leading cause of death without a treatment option at that time. In 2012, I joined the Alzheimer’s Association, eventually serving as vice president of public policy and fighting for better policies for patients, families, and caregivers. Despite my advocacy, I felt powerless to meaningfully change the course of disease for patients in my grandmother’s generation. What they needed was more research into Alzheimer’s and related dementias that yielded better care options.

ALZHEIMER'S STOLE PIECES OF OUR LIVES. A NEW TREATMENT IS GIVING US A FIGHTING CHANCE

At the time, research into diagnostics and disease-modifying treatments was tremendously weak. Experts from institutions like Northwestern and the University of Florida clamored for increased funding for Alzheimer’s research, while I traveled with patient advocates to Tallahassee and Washington, D.C., to garner support for desperately needed investment and better policy. We knew it was too late for many, but hoped the next generation would have better options.

Amazingly, advocacy from all corners of the country led to greater investment in research, and the past decade has yielded innovations that are transforming what is possible for people facing Alzheimer’s today.

ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION

New blood tests can identify the biological signs of Alzheimer's years before dementia becomes obvious, making earlier diagnosis possible. Emerging research is showing that simple lifestyle interventions can help support cognitive health as we age, especially when instituted early. 

We now have the first treatments shown to slow cognitive decline in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease. And promising next-generation clinical trials are exploring whether treating the disease even earlier—before significant symptoms develop—could delay or prevent cognitive decline.

These breakthroughs are transformative. For years, our challenge was advancing the science. Now, our challenge is ensuring patients can access these advances. That is the challenge I’m now focused on addressing.

NEWT GINGRICH: ALZHEIMER’S IS WAGING A WAR ON MILLIONS. CONGRESS COULD HELP US WIN IT

Today, as Florida’s Secretary of Elder Affairs, I lead efforts to serve older Floridians and their caregivers in a state with one of the nation’s largest populations of seniors. And now, as chair of the federal Advisory Council on Alzheimer’s Research, Care, and Services, I have overseen the development of practical policy recommendations on how our country can close that gap, continuing to accelerate innovation while ensuring advances make their way to the patients who need them.

Some of our most urgent recommendations focus on helping patients get diagnosed earlier. As it stands, Americans wait an average of three and a half years for a dementia diagnosis. By then, significant cognitive decline may have already occurred, limiting patients’ ability to benefit from interventions and treatment.

THE BEST TIME TO TALK TO YOUR PARENTS ABOUT SENIOR CARE — BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE

With better tools now available, it is time to modernize how we detect cognitive decline. Medicare should require standardized, validated cognitive assessment tools during initial and annual wellness visits, so every older American receives a consistent evaluation to catch decline early. 

Today, cognitive assessments vary widely across practices, allowing early signs of dementia, including Alzheimer's, to slip through the cracks during the window when intervention can make the greatest difference.

Congress should also pass the ASAP Act without delay, which would allow Medicare to cover U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved Alzheimer's diagnostic tests for eligible patients, helping ensure quick access to tests that can help confirm a diagnosis while time is still on their side.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

For the millions of families who have watched someone they love disappear to Alzheimer's or another dementia, these policies are more than abstract proposals. They create the possibility of more meaningful time for patients like my grandmother, who deserved more options than science could offer her.

For the first time in decades, better options are here. Now, our policies must catch up.

item.title: Kirk Cousins and No 1 pick Fernando Mendoza give Raiders bettors some hope in the upcoming year
item.description: Kirk Cousins and No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza headline a revamped Las Vegas Raiders quarterback room under new head coach Klint Kubiak this season.
item.content:encoded:
Las Vegas is the place you go with a lot of hope in your head and in your heart. This year, optimism reigns for the Raiders as they have new pieces that could prove that its endless rebuilding phase is drawing to a close and that a fresh era in Sin City is underway.

The Raiders suffered through a miserable 2025 campaign, finishing dead last in the division with a 3–14 record and securing the No. 1 overall pick in the draft. Not everything was bad; tight end Brock Bowers and pass rusher Maxx Crosby delivered individual, Pro Bowl-caliber dominance to keep games visually competitive. A drought on offense held the team back, as Las Vegas scored an NFL-worst 241 points on the season. An inability to protect the football, win on the road, or generate consistent quarterback play ultimately led to a quick, one-and-done exit for head coach Pete Carroll after the season finale.

TOM BRADY GIVES RAIDERS HARSH 'REALITY' CHECK AFTER THE TEAM WON ONLY THREE GAMES IN 2025

To fix the offensive structure, Las Vegas hired former Seahawks and Vikings offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak as head coach. He has shown a lot of success, and perhaps he can revamp an offense with a lot of talent at many positions. The front office then completely reshaped the quarterback room, making two massive moves: signing four-time Pro Bowler Kirk Cousins in free agency to a multi-year deal, and drafting top quarterback prospect Fernando Mendoza with the No. 1 overall pick in the NFL Draft. That did spell the end of time for Garner Minshew on the roster, but with Cousins and Mendoza, I doubt they will miss him.

RAIDERS NEW HEAD COACH KLINT KUBIAK NAMES KIRK COUSINS STARTING QB OVER NO. 1 PICK FERNANDO MENDOZA

Offensively, the unit gains stability, or at least a veteran and professional presence with Cousins operating behind an upgraded interior offensive line. With All-Pro tight end Bowers serving as the centerpiece alongside Michael Mayer and wideout Tre Tucker, the offense possesses far more execution upside than last fall—all while Mendoza develops behind the scenes. That doesn’t mention that Ashton Jeanty could make a major impact now that he has a reliable quarterback under center.

HOW KIRK COUSINS AND FERNANDO MENDOZA ARE BUILDING 'GREAT' RELATIONSHIP THROUGH RAIDERS WORK, FAITH AND MORE

Defensively, Crosby remains the focal point of the pass rush (even after he was traded and sent back in the offseason). He is now flanked by Kwity Paye up front and backed by an overhauled linebacking corps featuring Quay Walker and Nakobe Dean. If Taron Johnson and the secondary hold up against complex passing schemes, the unit should take a noticeable leap in efficiency.

If there is one thing you should count on this season, it is that the Raiders won’t be quite as bad as they were last season. Asking them to get to the playoffs is a bit of a stretch. They still have the Denver Broncos, Los Angeles Chargers and Kansas City Chiefs in their division. However, the pieces for progress are there.

Does that mean they get over the 5.5 wins this season? Hard to say. Cousins wasn’t very good in Atlanta, and they have a similar makeup to the Raiders. I do think Kubiak is a solid coach and should keep the ball moving. Mendoza is ready to take over if Cousins doesn’t succeed.

I’m banking on Jeanty to have a good year. He scored just five rushing touchdowns last season, but I think with a better quarterback and an offensive coordinator for a coach, he will get more looks. I think he scores over 7.5 rushing touchdowns. I also like his over 974.5 yards. You’re asking him to get exactly what he did last season with a worse team. The biggest concern with any of this is that the Raiders will be trailing frequently, but Kubiak may control the ball more, giving him more work.

item.title: College football Sunday picks feature Ole Miss moving on from Lane Kiffin and Notre Dame hosting Wisconsin
item.description: The first full Saturday of college football wraps up with Sunday picks for Ole Miss vs. Louisville and Notre Dame vs. Wisconsin at Lambeau Field.
item.content:encoded:
We’ve made it through the first full Saturday of college football. 

On the one hand, it is nice for college football to be back. On the other hand, I have put out three bad picks. I don't hate the reads, but I absolutely hate the results that I've had. Luckily, we have some Sunday football to enjoy, and this will be the last weekend without NFL football for a while. I have plays in two games today.

This is the best game on the slate for today, and arguably the entire weekend. It is the only matchup between two ranked teams, and there are plenty of reasons to be excited about it even if there weren’t little numbers listed next to each team. Louisville is looking to follow up a strong 9-4 campaign last year that ended with a win over Toledo in the Bush’s Boca Raton Bowl. 

I’m not sure if it is good or bad news, but the Cardinals added eight transfers to the starting lineup on offense. On the one hand, that could mean very talented players coming in. On the other hand, it means there could be a lot of confusion, and they had to replace a lot of players who may have left. Their defense also has five transfers.

WEEK ONE UPSET SPECIAL: THESE THREE COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS SHOULD BE ON UPSET ALERT THIS WEEKEND

For Ole Miss, the story from last year will certainly still be active this year. They had Lane Kiffin at the helm last year, and he left them to go coach LSU. Now they are coached by Pete Golding.

For them, this is a very important game. They need to move on from Kiffin as quickly as possible. Their team saw a lot of guys come over via the transfer portal as well, but they have more stability with Trinidad Chambliss under center again. There are just three players starting that came over from the transfer portal on offense. On defense, it is a totally different story. Of their starters, just four are returning from last year. Expect some confusion and issues on defense to start the season.

This game should be pretty entertaining. On one side, you have a new offense facing a new defense. On the other, you have an established quarterback who excelled at times last year facing a defense returning most of its starters. In some ways, it is still a new system for both teams. Chambliss also has a new coach. I think we are going to see a fairly low-scoring game. Give me the under at 55.5.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES ON HOT SEAT: BILL BELICHICK, MIKE NORVELL AND OTHERS FACING MAKE-OR-BREAK 2026

This game probably won’t be nearly as close as the one just covered, but there is still plenty of intrigue. Wisconsin is no longer a powerhouse, but it still has some good talent. The Badgers went just 4-8 last season while playing a really tough schedule. There are a lot of new faces on offense, with five transfers taking starting roles, including the quarterback, running back and two members of the offensive line.

Notre Dame is expected to be one of the best teams in the country. Seems a little easy when you’re not in a conference, and you can basically play anyone you want. CJ Carr will be under center again after last year’s 10-2 season. This season’s schedule looks like a bit of a joke. Miami is the only questionable game on the slate, and they host the Hurricanes this season. The backfield is turned over to Aneyas Williams, who had a decent enough year last year.

I’m taking the points with Wisconsin in this one. 

It isn’t that I think the Badgers are even close to as good as Notre Dame, but even though the Fighting Irish are technically the home team, the game is being played at Lambeau Field in Wisconsin. I think that will favor the Badgers. Also, under Marcus Freeman, the Fighting Irish are just 3-5 in the first two weeks of the season. They’ve lost the first game of the year in two of Freeman’s four years as head coach. I’ll take Wisconsin +20.5.

item.title: LSU had a revival, Clemson was at a funeral: Lane Kiffin’s debut sends a loud message to college football
item.description: Lane Kiffin's LSU debut delivered a 28-3 halftime lead over Clemson as Death Valley crowds rivaled the 2019 season in a star-studded spectacle.
item.content:encoded:
The Lane Kiffin era at LSU might have started with a hiccup by his team running out of the tunnel just a tad early on Saturday night, but they made up for it in front of a rabid crowd in "Death Valley" that reminded the head coach of Mardi Gras season.

If you thought a little rain was going to dampen the party in Baton Rouge, you were solely mistaken. If anything, the two-hour delay gave the raucous crowd a chance to catch their breath and reload after the pregame festivities looked more like something out of a Woodstock documentary.

Thousands of fans, six deep along the barricades, waited for this LSU team, led by Kiffin, to walk the streets just outside of Tiger Stadium. This was more of a revival, compared to a debut, and I know it's only one game.

"I felt like I was back at Mardi Gras," Lane Kiffin said following the 51-10 win over Clemson.

LANE KIFFIN KNOWS THERE AREN’T EXCUSES AT LSU. NOW COMES THE TEST OF MAKING IT WORTH THE PRICE OF ADMISSION

Police officers hadn’t seen this type of crowd in years, with two people mentioning the 2019 season as the last time the streets were this packed before kickoff. And, forget about Clemson fans making the trip south to Louisiana.

While one team is obsessed with their new coach, Clemson seemed complacent. The visitors section was essentially empty compared to other teams who have sat in the same corner of Tiger Stadium.

Once the loudspeakers started playing Garth Brooks, you knew that this night in Death Valley was going to be different. It did not feel like the Brian Kelly era, though that's probably not the best comparison.

Lane Kiffin walked the streets with his team in front of him, while Livvy Dunne and Theo Vonn trailed just behind the Tigers' head coach.

The star-studded night in Baton Rouge was fitting for the new king of Louisiana, who strolled onto the field in his double-breasted suit while waving at the student section. Everything about this beating felt like a Hollywood Red Carpet event, with congressional leaders and celebrities lining the sidelines.

And, after a long week for college football fans who were following the non-stop headlines surrounding the Louisiana court case, you just knew Kiffin was going to have something to say while heading into the locker room at halftime with a 28-3 lead over Clemson.

INSIDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM: SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN

"Imagine if we had pro players," the LSU head coach told ESPN.

Yeah, I don't know if that would have actually mattered tonight.

Why? Because we were watching two programs headed in opposite directions.

In what might end up being his last season at the helm if he doesn’t turn this thing around in quick fashion, the Clemson head coach can't really talk his way out of this one.

Everything about what we witnessed with this Tigers football team looks like a program who has lost its luster. There is nothing appealing about Clemson any longer, besides the head coach coming up with different ways to describe his team.

Just last week, Dabo made it a point to say he did not have any starters, making light of the fact he would find out how good his team was after they went up against LSU.

For the fans who have invested in this program, hoping that they would find their way out of the woods, tonight's performance shows just how far Clemson has fallen down the ladder. And, I don't see how those within the athletic department can come out of Baton Rouge with hope of a turnaround season.

CLEMSON'S DABO SWINNEY THROWS SHADE AT LANE KIFFIN, LSU OVER BRINGING IN NFL PLAYERS: 'IT'S EMBARRASSING'

Honestly, this brand will always have life thanks to what Swinney accomplished in the CFP's early years.

But now? This football program feels as though they are just too far gone.

On one side, you had an LSU fanbase invigorated by a new head coach and life that was injected into the rabid group of fans. For Clemson, watching them play LSU on Saturday night, in Kiffin's debut, felt like two different teams headed in two different directions.

Swinney spent the offseason complaining about Ole Miss tampering with one of his former players, and about how he wasn’t finished with the job at Clemson.

Now, that talk just looks cheap and underwhelming, with Swinney having to answer some very hard questions.

What some forget about the entire ordeal around a Louisiana court over the past ten days is that Lane Kiffin loves to put on a show.

The problem was that the SEC wasn’t buying a ticket.

When LSU was deciding on whether to roster at least three former 'professional players' after a Baton Rouge judge granted them an injunction this week, they were doing so knowing the SEC was ready to pounce on the program.

But, we all knew what story you'd be reading right now if LSU would have lost to Clemson on Saturday night.

item.title: Kushner, Witkoff set for Kyiv talks after Putin meeting in US push for peace
item.description: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Vladimir Putin for over three hours in Moscow before heading to Kyiv to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a day after meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow as part of efforts to end the war between the two countries.

Zelenskyy said Sunday morning that he had met with his negotiating team ahead of the Americans' arrival and that Kyiv was prepared for the discussions.

"Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A dignified character of the postwar peace is needed."

"Our proposals are ready," he added. "It is important to work in a coordinated, substantive, and realistic manner."

CIA DIRECTOR JOHN RATCLIFFE MET WITH RUSSIAN INTELLIGENCE OFFICIALS IN VISIT TO MOSCOW, KREMLIN SAYS

Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin for more than three hours behind closed doors Saturday, though the talks ended without any announced breakthroughs.

Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described the meeting as "constructive, frank and useful," but did not disclose specific outcomes.

A White House official said following the meeting that the two sides discussed "substantive plans for next steps," which are expected to be announced in the coming weeks. The official added that the U.S. delegation looked forward to "equally productive meetings" in Ukraine.

The Kyiv meeting comes as Washington seeks to revive efforts to reach a settlement in a war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Those efforts had lost momentum over the past six months as U.S. attention shifted to the war with Iran.

PUTIN AND IRAN 'NEED EACH OTHER DESPERATELY,' EXPERT SAYS, AS RUSSIA VOICES SUPPORT FOR REGIME

Significant differences between Moscow and Kyiv remain, including over territory. Kyiv has rejected Russia’s demand that Ukraine withdraw from portions of the eastern Donetsk and Luhansk regions that remain under Ukrainian control.

Ushakov said Moscow provided the U.S. delegation with its "comprehensive assessment" of the battlefield during Saturday's meeting, though the discussions extended beyond the war.

"Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail," Ushakov said.

President Donald Trump said Friday that he dispatched Witkoff and Kushner, his son-in-law and adviser, to determine whether progress toward a peace agreement could be made.

"We have an idea for peace. I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators," Trump told reporters. "They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it."

The diplomatic push comes as Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange drone and missile attacks. Both sides reported strikes overnight into Sunday despite agreeing to pause attacks on each other's capitals during the negotiations.

Fox News Digital’s Robert McGreevy and The Associated Press contributed to this report.
